subject: What Changed to Your Credit Card Today? Edition 8
summary: Axis Bank's late fee and forex markup hike spreads to eighteen more cards, including a real devaluation on the REWARDS card that strips out insurance covers. HSBC adds a welcome cashback to four cards, and Amex bumps up welcome bonuses on two.
body_html:
This is the biggest single day we've tracked so far, twenty-six changes across three issuers. Most of it is one story wearing eighteen different masks: Axis Bank is rolling the same late-fee and forex markup hike we first flagged on the Freecharge Plus and Airtel Axis cards back on 20 August out across most of its remaining card portfolio. Alongside that, HSBC added a small welcome cashback to four cards, and Amex quietly bumped up welcome bonuses on some cards while trimming reward wording on another. Let's take the Axis wave first since it's most of today's volume, then HSBC, then Amex.

AXIS BANK VISTARA Credit Card

This is the clearest version of the pattern repeating across Axis Bank's card book today, so worth spelling out once in full. The overdue penalty band that used to be a flat ₹1,200 for any total payment due above ₹10,000 is now split: ₹1,200 for dues between ₹10,001 and ₹50,000, and ₹1,300 for anything above ₹50,000. Separately, the Dynamic Currency Conversion (DCC) markup, the fee you pay when a transaction is billed to you in rupees by a foreign-registered merchant, more than doubled from 1.5% to 3.5% plus taxes.

Run the forex number: spend ₹1 lakh through a foreign-billed merchant in a year and your markup goes from about ₹1,500 to about ₹3,500, an extra ₹2,000 gone before you've spent a rupee on the actual purchase.

The catch: this only bites if you carry a balance past your due date or spend through DCC-billed transactions. Pay in full and avoid DCC billing (opt for the merchant's local currency where you have the choice) and this change costs you nothing.

LIC Axis Bank Platinum Credit Card

Narrower than the Vistara change: only the DCC markup moved here, 1.5% to 3.5% plus taxes on international transactions. Late fee tiers on this card are untouched today.

The catch: if you use this card abroad or for foreign-billed purchases, that's roughly ₹2,000 more per ₹1 lakh spent through DCC. If you don't, this is a non-event.

Miles and More Axis Bank Credit Card

Full standard pattern: ₹1,200 for dues between ₹10,001 and ₹50,000, ₹1,300 above that, and DCC markup up to 3.5% plus taxes.

The catch: same as the Vistara card above, this only costs you money if you carry a balance or spend through DCC billing.

Samsung Axis Bank Signature Credit Card

The ₹1,200 fee tier is unchanged at its lower bound, but a new ₹1,300 tier now kicks in above ₹50,000 due. DCC markup rises from 1.5% to 3.5%.

The catch: identical logic to the cards above, this is a cost only if you're carrying a balance above ₹50,000 or spending through DCC.

SpiceJet Axis Bank Voyage Credit Card

Standard pattern again: ₹1,200 for ₹10,001 to ₹50,000 due, ₹1,300 above ₹50,000, DCC markup to 3.5%.

The catch: the usual, this matters only if you don't clear your dues in full or you spend abroad through DCC-billed merchants.

Flipkart Axis Bank Super Elite Credit Card

Same standard pattern: ₹1,200 for the ₹10,001 to ₹50,000 band, ₹1,300 above it, DCC markup to 3.5%.

The catch: unchanged for anyone paying in full and avoiding DCC-billed transactions.

Axis Bank Pride Platinum Credit Card

Same pattern once more: ₹1,200 and ₹1,300 late fee tiers, DCC markup to 3.5%.

The catch: as above, a cost only for balance-carriers and international DCC spenders.

IndianOil Axis Bank Premium Credit Card

Standard pattern: ₹1,200 for ₹10,001 to ₹50,000, ₹1,300 above ₹50,000, DCC markup to 3.5%.

The catch: the usual condition, this only matters if you're not paying your statement in full each cycle.

Axis Bank Atlas Credit Card

Only the DCC markup changed here, 1.5% to 3.5% plus taxes. Late fee bands are untouched.

The catch: Atlas is a travel-focused card, so this one's worth noticing even if you always pay in full, since a lot of your spend on this card is probably foreign-billed. ₹2,000 extra per ₹1 lakh of DCC spend adds up fast on a travel card.

Privilege Easy Credit Card

Two things changed here, and the second is bigger than the standard fee hike. The overdue penalty and DCC markup moved the same way as the other cards above: ₹1,200 for ₹10,001 to ₹50,000 due, ₹1,300 above it, DCC up to 3.5%.

But the annual fee waiver got quietly harder to hit. Previously, only rent and wallet-load transactions were excluded from the spend threshold that earns your fee waiver. Now the exclusion list has grown to cover Utility & Telecom, Rent, Wallet, Government services, Insurance, Gold & Jewelry, Fuel, Education services, and Bridge, Road & Toll fees. If your spend mix leans on any of these categories to hit your waiver threshold, that spend no longer counts.

The catch: this is the real story on this card. Add up how much of your annual spend on this card falls into the newly excluded categories, if it's a meaningful chunk, you may need to spend more in other categories to still clear your fee waiver this year.

Cashback Credit Card

Full standard pattern applied: Nil up to ₹500 due, ₹500 for ₹501 to ₹5,000, ₹1,200 for ₹10,001 to ₹50,000, ₹1,300 above ₹50,000, and DCC markup to 3.5%.

The catch: as with the other standard-pattern cards, this only costs you if you're carrying a balance or spending through DCC.

HORIZON Credit Card

The recurring ₹100 charge for missing your Minimum Amount Due (MAD) for two consecutive cycles stays in place, just reworded for clarity. What's actually new is a ₹1,300 fee tier for dues above ₹50,000 (previously the ceiling was a flat ₹1,200), and the DCC markup rising from 1.5% to 3.5%.

The catch: if your dues regularly cross ₹50,000, that's an extra ₹100 per cycle you weren't paying before, on top of the DCC change.

Google Pay Flex Axis Bank Credit Card

Standard fee restructuring: the ₹1,200 band now applies specifically to ₹10,001 to ₹50,000 due (it used to apply to anything above ₹10,000), and a new ₹1,300 tier covers anything above ₹50,000. DCC markup rises to 3.5% (worded as 3.5% flat here, without the "plus taxes" language other cards use, worth confirming with Axis directly if this matters to you).

The catch: the usual condition applies, this bites only if you're carrying a balance or spending through DCC.

Axis Bank REWARDS Credit Card

This is the one card in today's Axis wave where the story is bigger than fees. Alongside the standard late fee restructuring (Nil up to ₹500, ₹500 for ₹501–5,000, ₹750 for ₹5,001–10,000, ₹1,200 for ₹10,001–50,000, ₹1,300 above ₹50,000) and the DCC markup rising to 3.5%, Axis stripped out a set of insurance and travel benefits entirely: purchase protection cover up to ₹1 lakh, credit shield of ₹1 lakh, and travel covers of up to $300 to $500 for delayed or lost check-in baggage and lost travel documents. Three merchant discounts also disappeared: 15% off flights and hotels via MakeMyTrip, 10% off Swiggy orders, and 10% off (up to ₹1,000) on Tira.

If you ever priced in that ₹1 lakh credit shield or the baggage cover when you travelled, that protection is gone now, not reduced, gone.

The catch: this is a genuine devaluation, not just a fee tweak. If any of these benefits, the insurance covers or the MakeMyTrip/Swiggy/Tira discounts, were a real part of why you use this card, it's worth comparing what else Axis or a competitor offers before your next renewal.

Axis Bank ACE Credit Card

Full standard tier restructuring: Nil up to ₹500, ₹500 for ₹501 to ₹5,000, ₹1,200 for ₹10,001 to ₹50,000, ₹1,300 above ₹50,000, and DCC markup to 3.5%.

The catch: the usual, only a cost if you carry a balance or spend through DCC billing.

Axis Bank My Zone Credit Card

Only the DCC markup changed, 1.5% to 3.5% plus taxes. Late fee tiers weren't touched in this update.

The catch: matters only if you spend internationally or through DCC-billed merchants on this card.

INDIANOIL AXIS BANK Credit Card

Standard pattern: ₹1,200 for ₹10,001 to ₹50,000 due, ₹1,300 above ₹50,000, DCC markup to 3.5%. Axis also added a "Read More" link to the terms page, a navigation tweak, not a benefit change.

The catch: the usual condition, this costs you only if you're carrying a balance or spending through DCC.

Neo Credit Card

Standard pattern to close out the Axis wave: ₹1,200 for ₹10,001 to ₹50,000, ₹1,300 above ₹50,000, DCC markup to 3.5%.

The catch: as with the rest of today's Axis cards, a cost only for balance-carriers and DCC spenders.

HSBC Taj Credit Card

New welcome cashback: spend ₹1,000 or more within 30 days of getting the card, after submitting your income documents through Account Aggregator, and get ₹1,000 cashback back. The offer is valid until 31 August 2026, so it's time-limited.

The catch: you have to complete the Account Aggregator income document submission for this to count, skip that step and the cashback doesn't trigger even if you hit the spend.

HSBC TravelOne Credit Card

Same offer structure as the Taj card: ₹1,000 cashback for ₹1,000 spend within 30 days, conditional on submitting income documents via Account Aggregator.

The catch: identical condition, the Account Aggregator step isn't optional paperwork, it's the gate for the cashback.

HSBC Premier Credit Card

Same ₹1,000-for-₹1,000 welcome cashback added here too, within 30 days of card issuance.

The catch: same Account Aggregator condition as the other HSBC cards in this batch.

HSBC Visa Platinum Credit Card

Fourth and final HSBC card to get the same ₹1,000 cashback on ₹1,000 spend within 30 days, gated on completing account aggregation.

The catch: this is a genuinely easy ₹1,000 to earn if you're a new cardholder anyway, ₹1,000 of spend in 30 days is a low bar, but don't forget the Account Aggregator step or you'll do the spend for nothing.

American Express® Corporate Gold Card

No real change here despite showing up in today's diff. The reward earn rate (1 point per ₹50 on business spend, 1 point per ₹100 on fuel, utility, telecom, wholesale, and insurance spend, capped at 1,000 points a month) is unchanged, Amex just rephrased the wording for clarity.

The catch: none, this one's a wording cleanup, not a benefit change.

American Express® Gold Card

New welcome gift added: 4,000 bonus Membership Rewards points for new cardholders.

The catch: check the exact spend or activation condition attached to this welcome gift on Amex's terms page before assuming it's unconditional, welcome gifts on Amex cards typically require a minimum spend within a set window.

American Express Membership Rewards® Credit Card

New welcome gift: 4,000 bonus Membership Rewards points for new cardholders, matching the Gold card's welcome gift.

The catch: same as above, confirm the activation spend condition before counting on this.

American Express SmartEarn™ Credit Card

New welcome cashback: ₹500 for spending ₹10,000 within the first 90 days of getting the card.

The catch: ₹10,000 in 90 days is roughly ₹3,300 a month, an easy bar for most new cardholders, but the cashback won't trigger if you fall short even by a little.

What I'd actually do with this

If you hold any of the eighteen Axis Bank cards in today's list, the core question is the same across almost all of them: do you carry a balance past your due date, or spend through DCC-billed transactions? If the answer to both is no, today's changes cost you nothing. If either is yes, set up autopay for your full statement amount, not just the minimum, and where you have the choice, opt to pay in the merchant's local currency instead of DCC billing in rupees.

Two cards need a closer look regardless of your payment habits. If you hold the Axis Bank REWARDS card, the insurance and travel covers you may have counted on for protection are gone, not reduced, so check what you're actually protected by now before you travel next. If you hold Privilege Easy, recheck your spend mix against the newly excluded categories to make sure you're still on track for your annual fee waiver.

If you hold any of the four HSBC cards, the ₹1,000-for-₹1,000 cashback is easy money if you're a new cardholder, just don't skip the Account Aggregator income document step, it's the one condition that actually gates the payout.

If you hold an Amex Gold, Membership Rewards, or SmartEarn card, these are straightforward wins with standard activation-spend conditions, worth checking the exact terms but nothing to be wary of here.

This is my honest read, not formal financial advice. I'm not your advisor, and before you make a call on any of this, run it past a professional or at least sleep on it. But this is exactly how I'd think about it if these were my cards.

If either is yes, set up autopay for your full statement amount, not just the minimum, and where you have the choice, opt to pay in the merchant's local currency instead of DCC billing in rupees. Two cards need a closer look regardless of your payment habits. If you hold any of the four HSBC cards, the ₹1,000-for-₹1,000 cashback is easy money if you're a new cardholder, just don't skip the Account Aggregator income document step, it's the one condition that actually gates the payout. If you hold an Amex Gold, Membership Rewards, or SmartEarn card, these are straightforward wins with standard activation-spend conditions, worth checking the exact terms but nothing to be wary of here.
